opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people underestimate is how big the gap is between a demo and a product. You can get a robot to do almost anything once on video — fold a shirt, load a dishwasher, pick a part off a conveyor. That's genuinely impressive, and the progress there has been real. But a demo that works eight out of ten times is a party trick. A product has to work basically every time, because the failures are what define the experience.

Think about it from the customer's side. If a factory deploys a robot that succeeds 95% of the time, that sounds great until you realize it means someone has to babysit it. If a person has to stand nearby to fix the one-in-twenty failure, you haven't saved that person's labor. You've just changed their job from doing the task to supervising a machine doing the task, which is often worse. The economics only flip when the reliability gets high enough that you can actually walk away. That's usually two or three more nines than people expect.

And homes are even harder, because the environment isn't controlled at all. In a factory you can at least engineer the world around the robot: fixtures, consistent lighting, known parts. In a home every kitchen is different, things move around, there's a dog, there's a kid's toy on the floor. So you're taking the hardest version of the long-tail problem and adding stakes on top. A robot that breaks a glass once a week isn't something anyone keeps.

The other piece is that reliability compounds over long tasks. If each step of a twenty-step task is 98% reliable, the whole task fails a third of the time. So for anything genuinely useful, which tends to mean multi-step, you need each individual skill to be extremely robust, and you need the system to notice when it's made a mistake and recover rather than just plowing ahead.

So to me capability isn't really the bottleneck anymore. We can show robots doing remarkable things. The bottleneck is getting from "it can" to "it will, every time, without a human watching." That's where most of the hard engineering lives, and it's the part that decides whether robots actually leave the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says 95% success may still require babysitting and that a robot breaking a glass is unacceptable, but it does not clearly state that even 99% success is inadequate because failures can cause physical damage.

r002.rationale: It identifies reliability as the bottleneck and mentions moving beyond 95% by “two or three more nines,” but does not clearly frame improving from roughly 95% to 99.9% as the central unresolved question.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this comes from having actually tried to ship robots into real environments, first at Cobalt with security robots roaming office buildings, and the thing you learn very fast is that the demo is maybe five percent of the problem. Getting a robot to do something impressive once is almost easy now. The hard part is getting it to do that same thing ten thousand times in a row, in a building it's never seen, with lighting that changed, with a chair someone left in the hallway, with the Wi-Fi dropping out, and having it fail gracefully when it doesn't work.

And the reason that matters so much economically is that the value of a robot is really a function of how little attention it needs. If a factory robot works 95% of the time, that sounds great, but it means a human has to be standing nearby to unstick it one time in twenty. At that point you haven't removed the human, you've just given them a more boring job. The same thing is true in a home, maybe even more so. Nobody wants a robot that folds laundry beautifully four days out of five and then drops a glass on the fifth. The cost of the failures dominates the value of the successes.

So when people ask why we don't have robots everywhere yet, I don't think it's primarily a hardware problem, and it's increasingly less of a "can the model understand the scene" problem. It's the long tail. It's the same lesson self-driving cars taught everyone: the last few percent of reliability takes more work than the first ninety, and it's where all the actual deployment risk lives.

What's interesting to me now, coming from the language model side, is that the way you attack that tail is changing. You used to hand-code recovery behaviors for every edge case you could think of, and you'd always be missing the ones you didn't think of. With foundation models you get something closer to common sense, so the robot can reason about a situation it was never explicitly trained on. That doesn't make reliability free, but it shifts the problem from enumerating failures to building systems that can recognize when they're uncertain and either recover or ask for help. That's the piece I think is going to unlock it.

r001.rationale: The response says 95% reliability still requires human intervention and gives a dropped-glass example, but it does not explain that even 99% success can be inadequate.

r002.rationale: It describes the long tail and says the last few percent take more work, but does not identify improving reliability from roughly 95% to 99.9% as the central unresolved question.

astra-6.text:
Because doing something once is very different from doing it reliably enough that someone can depend on it. You can have a really impressive demo where a robot picks up an object or completes a household task. But if it needs a person to intervene every ten attempts, you haven’t really automated the work. You’ve given someone a robot to supervise.

And that gets harder when you chain actions together. If each step succeeds 99 percent of the time, a task with a hundred steps only succeeds end to end about 37 percent of the time. So even what sounds like very good performance at the individual-action level can be frustratingly unreliable in practice.

Factories give you more control over the environment, but downtime is expensive. Homes are much less predictable: objects move, lighting changes, and people do things you didn’t anticipate. The robot has to handle those variations, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover. That’s the gap between a compelling demonstration and something you can actually leave to do useful work.

r001.rationale: The response says 99% success per step can yield only about 37% end-to-end success, but it does not say the remaining failures can cause physical damage.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability generally, but does not identify improving reliability from roughly 95% to 99.9% as a central unresolved question.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a robot doing something impressive once is very different from a robot doing something useful every day. In a demo, you can show the successful attempt. In a home or a factory, the robot has to handle all the little variations: an object is in a different place, something slips, someone walks in front of it. And when something goes wrong, it has to recover.

The difficulty compounds when you put a task together. If each step succeeds 99 percent of the time, that sounds great. But over a hundred steps, you only have about a 37 percent chance of getting through the whole thing without a failure. If a person has to keep coming over to reset the robot, you lose a lot of the value of automation.

So the question isn’t just, can it perform the task? It’s, how long can it keep working without help, and can it recognize and recover from its own mistakes? That’s what makes the difference between a compelling demonstration and something people can depend on.

r001.rationale: The response says that 99% success across many steps can still mean frequent failures, but it does not explain that those failures can cause physical damage.

r002.rationale: It discusses sustained reliability and recovery, but does not identify improving reliability from roughly 95% to 99.9% as a central unresolved question.
